newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK CROWN FALLS SHARPLY, SEEN WEAKENING FURTHER.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK CROWN FALLS SHARPLY, SEEN WEAKENING FURTHER.

text.p: The Slovak crown sharply weakened in nervous Tuesday morning trade, reacting to Czech crown movements, with dealers saying market sentiment remained bearish.
The crown lost some 300 basis points in the first trading hour, moving to around -3.80 percent versus its mark/dollar basket parity, from an opening level at some -0.80 percent.
"Though local banks still quote only small volumes, up to $1 million, foreigners are selling (Czech and Slovak) crowns and we have to react to it with price movements," said one trader.

The Czech National Bank (CNB) on Monday night cancelled the fluctuation band within it used to fix the Czech crown. The Czech crown subsequently fell to record low levels of around 10 percent on the depreciation side of its former basket.
"We think the crown will further decline but it's very hard to say were will it find a floor," the dealer added.
Another Bratislava-based dealer said the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) fixing at around midday is likely to be the strongest factor determining further crown's trend.

"Even if banks will not go to the central bank to complement their hard currency positions, since they are still trading only small volumes, the fixing will be a psychological point showing where the NBS wants to see the crown and where local banks can expect support," he added.
Tibor Fratrik of ING Bank said it was hard to say what was the crown's real price due to market's low liquidity.
"The price has fallen on low volumes and the money market is still highly illiquid, so the banks will, again, wait for the NBS fixing to show the trend," Fratrik said.

The Czech crown and its Slovak counterpart have been under strong speculative pressure, started by foreign banks, over the past two weeks, prompting the CNB to directly intervene several times on the market to prop up the ailing currency.

The NBS, however, has so far used only indirect intervention through its daily fixing, but at the same time it moved to limit liquidity on the local money market to prevent speculators from obtaining funds for short-selling crowns.
